newsitem.title: UK: British opposition matches Conservatives on tax.
newsitem.headline: British opposition matches Conservatives on tax.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party on Monday committed itself to maintaining the low-tax, low-spending profile of the Conservatives whom it hopes to replace in government within months.

Economics spokesman Gordon Brown boosted his image as a tough finance-minister-in-waiting by pledging that under him, the Treasury would tolerate neither an increase in public spending nor a rise in personal taxation.

"I will be making commitments for our (election) manifesto which are commitments for a parliament, and the basic rate and the top rate of (income) tax will remain unchanged," Brown told BBC radio in advance of making a keynote speech.
Britain's 23 percent basic income tax rate and 40 percent top rate are among the lowest in Europe.
There had been speculation that Labour, which has traditionally used tax to create a more equal society, would introduce a 50 percent rate on very high earners.

But Brown said: "It is because we understand the importance of work that there will be no return to penal marginal tax rates at the top. As a signal of our intentions, I want to make clear that we will not introduce a new top rate of tax."
Instead Brown said that when possible, Labour would introduce a 10 percent starting rate of income tax to benefit low-income families.
Brown also said he would accept the tough public spending targets already announced for the next two financial years by Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke.
"No credible chancellor would do anything other than what I will do, which is to have tough controls on public spending. I have to accept the need for prudence," he said.

And according to newspaper reports, he will say in his speech that he will maintain a current freeze on pay for government workers despite that fact that Labour is heavily bankrolled by public sector trade unions.
The pledges leave Labour dependent mainly on its planned "windfall tax" on the excess profits of utility companies privatised by the Conservatives for money to devote to their cherished objectives.

Brown is now thought to be planning to raise 10 billion pounds ($17 billion) from this one-off tax, using this largely to launch a massive drive to tackle the twin problems of long-term unemployment and jobless school leavers.
He believes this would cut government spending on unemployment benefit and welfare, enabling resources to be rechanneled into areas such as education.

Brown's pledges are convincing proof of the transformation of Labour under moderate leader Tony Blair. A party once committed to public ownership of the "commanding heights of the economy" is now discussing how to run capitalism more humanely.
With an election expected on May 1, if not before, the opinion polls continue to indicate that the public approves.
The latest poll, in the Sunday Times, gave Labour a 17 percentage point lead over the Conservatives, down two points from a month earlier.
